1401.title: The name that became a greeting
1401.hook: an old teacher calls himself only the drum-beater, and the young yogi from the road gets a new name
1401.carry: jay swaminarayan: every hello remembers god
1401.howItsDone: Swaminarayan followers greet one another with 'Jay Swaminarayan' and chant the Swaminarayan mantra in daily worship, remembering how Ramanand Swami initiated Nilkanth as Sahajanand Swami.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a seeker's road leads to a guru began with Nilkanth, the boy who walked across India with his questions until he reached the ashram at Loj.
screen: `NILKANTH REACHES LOJ.`

segments.voice: Jay Swaminarayan. In Swaminarayan homes and temples, it's how followers of this tradition say hello, how they say goodbye, and often how they answer the phone. Two words, run together into one name. But whose name is it? The young yogi who walked into Loj didn't arrive with it. He was Ghanshyam as a child, Nilkanth on the road. Somewhere between that ashram and the greeting on the phone, a name was given, and then a mantra. Today, how the boy from the road became Swaminarayan.
screen: `JAY SWAMINARAYAN` → `A GREETING AND A NAME` → `WHOSE NAME IS IT?`

segments.voice: Ramanand Swami, whose ashram Nilkanth had reached, was a respected guru in Gujarat with followers of his own. When the two met, tradition says Ramanand saw something rare in the young man. He'd once described himself, the story goes, as only the drum-beater, the one who calls the crowd before the real performer arrives. Ramanand initiated Nilkanth as a sadhu and gave him a new name: Sahajanand Swami, the one whose joy comes naturally. Before long, he chose this newcomer to lead the whole fellowship after him. Tradition says that soon after Ramanand died, Sahajanand gave his followers a new name to chant: Swaminarayan. Swami, master. Narayan, a name of God. As people chanted it, they began to call him by it too. Here the communities that follow him say different things, and say them with care. For some, both words point to him: Sahajanand himself is Swami and Narayan, the Lord. For others, Swami names Gunatitanand Swami, whom they hold as the ideal devotee, and Narayan names Sahajanand. They share the mantra, the greeting and the love for him. Behind all of this sits one of Hinduism's oldest practices: japa, saying a name of God again and again, often on a mala of beads, so the mind keeps coming home to God. Followers chant Swaminarayan this way. And the greeting carries the same idea out the front door. Jay Swaminarayan: victory to Swaminarayan. Every hello, every goodbye, every phone call is one more time the name is said. A greeting that is also a remembering.
screen: `RAMANAND, THE DRUM-BEATER` · `NILKANTH BECOMES SAHAJANAND` · `THE MANTRA: SWAMINARAYAN` · `JAPA: GOD'S NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN` · `EVERY HELLO REMEMBERS`

segments.voice: Followers of this tradition chant Swaminarayan on a mala, one bead for each name. Try it with your breath instead of beads: say a name inwardly on the in-breath, rest on the out-breath. If you pray in this tradition, use the mantra itself; if you pray in another, a name of God you love; if you don't pray, the name of someone you're grateful for. When the mind wanders, come back to the name.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, how Nilkanth became Sahajanand Swami under Ramanand, and how the mantra Swaminarayan, said in japa and in every greeting, became his name. Today's word.
screen: `GUJARAT'S SWAMINARAYAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: jay swaminarayan, every hello remembers God. A greeting that carries a name, and a name that carries a story. Until next time.

1402.title: Ekantik dharma: four together
1402.hook: a scripture made of questions asked out loud in a village courtyard, and a love for God that needs three companions
1402.carry: ekantik dharma: dharma, self-knowledge, detachment and bhakti together
1402.tomorrow: A letter that begins with no harm
1402.howItsDone: In Swaminarayan mandirs and homes, passages from the Vachanamrut are read aloud and explained at gatherings, and devotees study it together.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nilkanth became Sahajanand, and his mantra became a greeting. Jay Swaminarayan: every hello remembers God.
screen: `EVERY HELLO REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Evening in a village in Gujarat. A courtyard, a raised seat, a crowd on the ground: farmers, merchants, robed sadhus, children at the edges. The teacher on the seat is Swaminarayan, and he invites questions. Someone asks a hard one. Why does the mind keep running back to the same old cravings, even after years of devotion? He answers. Someone pushes back. He answers again. And off to one side, a few senior sadhus listen very closely, because they're going to write this down. Today, a holy book that began as a conversation.
screen: `A COURTYARD AT EVENING.` → `SOMEONE ASKS A HARD ONE.` → `SOMEONE WRITES IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: The book is the Vachanamrut. Followers hear the title as vachan, words, and amrut, the nectar of immortality: nectar in the form of words. They hold it as scripture, his own teaching, gathered from talks in Gadhada and other villages, each headed with the place, the setting, even what he was wearing that evening. First, its shape. It arrives as dialogue. A devotee asks, Swaminarayan answers, and sometimes he turns it around and asks the room. Then, the questions. How do you know if your devotion is real? What do you do with anger toward someone in your own community? Why does a person who has heard good teaching still not change? Kitchen-table questions, treated as worth a scripture. Last, the answer at its heart, which the tradition calls ekantik dharma: a whole-hearted life held up by four things together. Dharma, doing what's right. Knowing the self, the atman, as distinct from the body. Vairagya, detachment. And bhakti, love for God. Many teachers in the tradition read the four this way: love for God without right conduct goes hollow; detachment without love goes dry; knowing the self without devotion can turn proud. Picture the legs of a cot. Take one away and the whole thing tips. So when someone in the courtyard asks why old cravings keep coming back after years of devotion, the answer, read this way, isn't only pray harder. It's look at all four.
screen: `VACHANAMRUT — NECTAR IN WORDS` · `A SCRIPTURE THAT BEGINS AS DIALOGUE` · `EKANTIK DHARMA` · `DHARMA · THE SELF · DETACHMENT · BHAKTI` · `ALL FOUR, TOGETHER`

segments.voice: Give one breath to each leg of the cot: doing what's right, knowing yourself as more than the body, letting go, and love, for one face or, if you pray, for God. Then notice, without judging, which leg feels steady today and which one wobbles, and rest on the whole cot for a few breaths.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the Vachanamrut, his teaching kept as questions and answers, and its heart: ekantik dharma, four things held together. Today's word.
screen: `GUJARAT'S SWAMINARAYAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ekantik dharma, dharma, self-knowledge, detachment and bhakti together. In his courtyard, love for God never stood alone. See you tomorrow.

1403.title: A letter that begins with no harm
1403.hook: a teacher writes a short letter for people he will never meet, and among its first rules is no harm
1403.howItsDone: Swaminarayan devotees keep the Shikshapatri's ahimsa in a vegetarian, alcohol-free home, offer their food to God before eating, and read the Shikshapatri daily or hear it read aloud at gatherings.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vachanamrut's heart. Ekantik dharma: dharma, self-knowledge, detachment and bhakti together.
screen: `ALL FOUR, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: A conversation only reaches the people in the courtyard. So what about everyone else? The farmer three villages over who couldn't come. The family that moved away for work. The devotee born long after the teacher is gone. Tradition says Swaminarayan sat down at Vadtal, in Gujarat, and wrote them all a letter: short, in Sanskrit verse, something a person could carry and live by. It's called the Shikshapatri. And among the first rules it gives every follower, before much else, is this: harm no living being. Today, a letter that begins with no harm.
screen: `THE ONES WHO COULDN'T COME.` → `A SHORT LETTER IN VERSE.` → `FIRST: HARM NO LIVING BEING.`

segments.voice: Shiksha means instruction. Patri is a letter. Followers hold it as his own writing, and many Swaminarayan communities honor the day it was written, remembered as Vasant Panchami, the spring festival. Its first big teaching has a name every Hindu knows: ahimsa, non-harm. It's one of the oldest ideals in Hinduism; the Yoga Sutras put it first among the restraints a seeker keeps. What the Shikshapatri does is bring it down into an ordinary day. In paraphrase, it asks followers not to kill any living being, not even small creatures, and not to eat meat or drink alcohol. Harm can come out of a mouth too, so it asks them not to speak abusively, not to lie and not to steal. It speaks of serving one's parents and giving to those in need. Next, who it's for. Householders and sadhus, married women and widows, even rulers. Each life gets guidance that fits it, and none is left outside ahimsa. Last, how it asks to be used: read every day, and for those who can't read, heard read aloud, with respect. This is why Swaminarayan families, like many Hindu families, keep a vegetarian kitchen. It isn't a diet. It's a promise not to harm, kept three times a day at the table. In Gujarat, in London, in New Jersey, followers still open the same short letter and read what that promise asks.
screen: `SHIKSHAPATRI — A LETTER OF INSTRUCTION` · `AHIMSA — NO HARM` · `AT THE TABLE, IN SPEECH, IN THE HANDS` · `GUIDANCE FOR EVERY LIFE` · `READ IT EVERY DAY`

segments.voice: Think of the last meal you ate, and walk it back: the hands that cooked it, the field it grew in, the lives it touched. For a few breaths, simply notice, without judging, where it did no harm and where it may have. Swaminarayan families offer their food to God before they eat. If you pray, offer your next meal that way in your mind; if you don't, let one quiet thank-you stand in for it.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the Shikshapatri, his short letter, and its first teaching: ahimsa, no harm, kept in everyday life. Today's word.
screen: `GUJARAT'S SWAMINARAYAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ahimsa, lived at every meal. A short letter asks no harm, and a kitchen keeps the promise. Until tomorrow.

1404.title: How Narada caught devotion
1404.hook: a maid's son sweeps the floor while holy men sing of God, and devotion takes root
1404.carry: satsang: devotion is caught in holy company
1404.howItsDone: Swaminarayan devotees gather in weekly satsang assemblies at mandirs and in homes, with singing, readings from the scriptures and talks by sadhus or senior devotees.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shikshapatri, a short letter that begins with no harm. Ahimsa, lived at every meal.
screen: `NO HARM, AT EVERY MEAL.`

segments.voice: Long ago, in a house where holy men stayed through the rainy season, there was a small boy, the son of a maid. He swept, he fetched water, he sat quietly at the edge of the room while they sang and talked about God. Sometimes, with their permission, he ate what was left on their plates. He was only a child. But something was happening to him. The Bhagavata Purana says that boy became, in another life, Narada, the wandering sage with the veena who sings God's names through the worlds. Today, how devotion is caught.
screen: `A MAID'S SON, SWEEPING.` → `HOLY MEN SINGING OF GOD.` → `HE BECOMES NARADA.`

segments.voice: Narada tells this story himself, to the sage Vyasa. He says it was hearing those holy men, day after day, that woke love for God in him. Soon after, his mother died, and he set out alone. In a forest, he sat under a tree, remembered what he'd heard, and the Lord appeared in his heart for a moment, then was gone. A voice told him the longing would stay, and it did, into his next life. This is the teaching called satsang. Sat is the true, the real, the good. Sang is company. Satsang is the company of the true: holy people, God, good words. Many teachers put it simply: devotion is caught more than it's taught. You sit near people who love God, and love for God starts in you. That's why Hindu families gather in living rooms to sing bhajans and call it a satsang. In the Swaminarayan tradition the word goes further. A devotee is a satsangi. The weekly gathering is a satsang sabha. The whole fellowship, in Gujarat and far from it, is spoken of as the satsang. In the Vachanamrut, Swaminarayan speaks of keeping company with God and with a true sadhu, a holy person who lives the teaching. So satsang isn't only a community's name. It's the method. You come, you sit, you serve, you listen, even when you follow only part of it. A small boy at the edge of the room was enough to begin.
screen: `NARADA'S BOYHOOD` · `SAT — TRUE; SANG — COMPANY` · `DEVOTION IS CAUGHT` · `SATSANGI, SATSANG SABHA` · `COME, SIT, SERVE, LISTEN`

segments.voice: Bring back a room where people were singing to God or speaking of something good, a temple, a living room, a school assembly, and sit at its edge in your mind, the way the boy did. Let one line of a song, or one voice from that room, come back to you, and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, let it be a bhajan you know; if you don't, the voice of someone whose goodness rubbed off on you.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, satsang, the company of the true, which woke devotion in Narada and names the whole Swaminarayan fellowship. Today's word.

1405.title: Songs that keep God close
1405.hook: a sadhu sings his teacher from head to foot, and the song is still sung after the evening lamps
1405.carry: kirtan: singing god's form keeps him near
1405.howItsDone: Swaminarayan devotees sing kirtans by the tradition's poet-sadhus at mandir gatherings and at home, including songs that describe Swaminarayan's form and his daily life.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narada's boyhood in the Bhagavata. Satsang: devotion is caught in holy company.
screen: `DEVOTION IS CAUGHT.`

segments.voice: A harmonium, a pair of small cymbals, a handful of voices in a mandir after the evening lamps. The song is a kind of portrait. It moves slowly over one person, the way an eye moves over a face it loves: the forehead, the eyes, the smile, the hands, the feet. The man who first sang it wasn't a painter. He was a sadhu, one of a circle of poets who traveled with Swaminarayan and turned what they saw into songs. Today, the last day in Gujarat: the poet-sadhus, and the songs they left behind.
screen: `AFTER THE EVENING LAMPS.` → `A PORTRAIT IN A SONG.` → `A CIRCLE OF POETS.`

segments.voice: Tradition remembers several by name. Muktanand Swami, the elder disciple who welcomed Nilkanth at Loj. Premanand Swami, a singer and musician. Nishkulanand Swami, who also told his teacher's life in the Bhaktachintamani. Their songs are kirtan, praise sung together, and they're still sung in Swaminarayan mandirs and homes. First, songs of watching. Tradition says Premanand sang Swaminarayan's form from head to foot, and the shape of his day: how he rose, how he bathed, how he sat with the people who came to see him. For his followers he is God, Narayan, so these songs are a darshan you can carry: seeing the beloved with your eyes shut. This is one of bhakti's oldest ways, smarana, remembering. Across Hindu traditions, devotees sing God's form in loving detail, so the heart has something to hold. Swaminarayan devotees sing these songs at night, so the day ends with God close. Then, songs of longing, in the voice of a devotee who misses the beloved and can't bear the distance. Longing isn't a failure of faith here. It's part of love, and the poets give it a tune. Then, songs of letting go. Nishkulanand's verses press on vairagya, detachment. In paraphrase, one says that giving things up doesn't hold unless detachment has reached the heart. And that's where Gujarat ends: a boy on the road, a name that became a greeting, four things held together, a letter of no harm, a company of the true, and a circle of poets singing God close.

1406.title: Namdev's kite string
1406.hook: a song from a Marathi tailor turns up in Punjab, and a boy keeps his eye on a kite string
1406.carry: simran: the mind on god, like a kite string
1406.howItsDone: Namdev's hymns are sung by Varkaris in Maharashtra and, from the Guru Granth Sahib, in gurdwaras; in Ghuman, Punjab, a shrine honors him.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poet-sadhus. Kirtan: singing God's form keeps him near. Gujarat ends here, and Punjab begins.
screen: `SONGS THAT KEEP GOD CLOSE.`

segments.voice: A boy on a rooftop is flying a paper kite. His friends are around him, laughing, teasing, talking over each other, and he's laughing with them. But watch his hands, his eyes. Whatever he's saying, part of him never leaves the string. That picture comes from a song by Namdev, the tailor-saint of Maharashtra this path met last year, singing to Vitthal. And the song is kept far to the north, in Punjab, in a book Sikhs honor as their living Guru. Today, Punjab, where devotional songs from many places ended up living side by side.
screen: `A BOY AND A KITE.` → `A SONG FROM MAHARASHTRA.` → `KEPT IN PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: Punjab is a crossroads, and the songs show it. First, the book. The Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs revere as their Guru, holds the hymns of the Sikh Gurus, and also songs by bhagats, devotees from outside that line: Namdev from Maharashtra, Kabir the weaver of Kashi, Ravidas, and Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of Punjab, among others. Sikhs sing them in the gurdwara beside the Gurus' own hymns. Hindus honor Namdev, Kabir and Ravidas in their own traditions too. So here is ground both share, each standing on it in its own way. Then, Namdev himself. Tradition says that late in life he traveled north and lived in Punjab, and a village there, Ghuman, remembers him with a shrine. A tailor from the Marathi country, honored in a Punjabi village. And now the kite. In paraphrase, the hymn gives a string of pictures. A boy flies his kite and talks with his friends, but his mind stays on the string. Young women carry water pots on their heads, laughing and chatting as they walk, but their attention stays on the pot. A cow grazes far out in the fields, her mind on her calf. A mother goes about her work, her heart on the child in the cradle. That, the song says, is how the mind can stay on God: not by stopping life, but in the middle of it. Hindus call this smarana, remembering God; Sikhs call it simran, keeping the Name in mind. Two traditions, one practice, kept in one song. The talk goes on. Underneath, one thread holds.
screen: `PUNJAB, A CROSSROADS OF SONG` · `SAINTS FROM MANY PLACES IN ONE BOOK` · `NAMDEV REMEMBERED IN A PUNJAB VILLAGE` · `THE MIND ON THE STRING` · `SMARANA · SIMRAN`

segments.voice: Let sounds come and go around you, the way friends chatter around the boy on the roof, and keep one light thread of attention on a name, the way his fingers stay on the string. If you pray, let it be a name of God you love: Vitthal, as Namdev sang, or Waheguru, as Sikhs say; if you don't, let the thread be your breath. When you notice you've let go, pick the string back up.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namdev's boy on the roof. Simran: the mind on God, like a kite string.
screen: `THE MIND ON THE STRING.`

segments.voice: A small shop in Banaras. The smell of leather, a low bench, a man bent over a shoe with an awl in his hand. This is Ravidas, the cobbler-saint, whom this path first met on day ninety-five. A neighbor leans in the doorway. It's a holy day, he says. Everyone's going down to the Ganga to bathe. Come with us. Ravidas looks at the shoe in his hands. In one telling, he has promised it to a customer by tonight. Today, a cobbler who has to decide whether to put down his work.
screen: `A COBBLER'S BENCH IN BANARAS.` → `COME TO THE GANGA.` → `A SHOE PROMISED BY TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the story people tell. Ravidas doesn't go. He tells his neighbor, in a line people still quote: if the mind is pure, the Ganga is in this bowl, the leatherworker's bowl of water by his bench. In some tellings he gives the neighbor a coin to offer the river, but only if the Ganga reaches out and takes it herself. At the river, the story says, a hand rises from the water and takes it. First, the bench. The story isn't against pilgrimage. Ravidas honors the Ganga; that's why the coin goes. What it teaches is one of bhakti's biggest ideas: what brings a person near God is a pure heart and love, not birth, caste or place. Ravidas was born into a leatherworking caste that others treated as untouchable, and still the river came to his bench. Then, the song. His hymns are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in one he sings of a city called Begampura, the town without sorrow. In paraphrase: no one there is anxious or afraid, no tax weighs on anyone, no one is ranked second or third, and anyone may walk where they please. A world where the cobbler and everyone else stand as equals. Last, Punjab. Ravidas lived in Banaras, but in Punjab you'll hear him called Guru Ravidas, and his birthday is kept with processions and hymn singing. Hindus honor him, Sikhs sing his hymns from their scripture, and communities who take his name honor him as their own Guru. Each comes to him in its own way. And the week behind: a greeting, a letter, a company, a song, a kite string, a cobbler's bowl. Every one brings God into an ordinary day.
screen: `IF THE MIND IS PURE, THE GANGA IS HERE` · `A PURE HEART, NOT BIRTH OR PLACE` · `BEGAMPURA, THE TOWN WITHOUT SORROW` · `HONORED IN PUNJAB IN MANY WAYS`

segments.voice: Rest your hands where your work happens, on a desk, a counter or your knees, and think of the work in front of you this week, cooking, code, care, cleaning: let it be the bench.
